source.title: All Circuits Lead to Rome: Rethinking Functional Anisotropy in Circuit and Sheaf Discovery for LLMs
source.authors: Xi Chen; Ming-Yu Jin; Jing-Cheng Niu; Yu-Tong Yin; Jin-Man Zhao; Bang-Wei Guo; Dimitris N. Metaxas; Zhao-Ran Wang; Yu-Tao Yue; Gerald Penn

page_placements.theme: Faithful edge circuits can be structurally non-unique

record.tranche_reason: The study's own IOI experiments find multiple structurally distinct task-performing sheaves and challenge treating one discovered subgraph as the unique or essential mechanism. It also compares circuit-discovery methods and shows evaluation outcomes depend on method and settings.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates newly discovered IOI sheaves and several circuit-discovery methods; it does not rerun the original 26-head circuit's specific head-role patching tests or knock out everything outside that exact circuit. Its discussion of backup name-mover heads cites prior work rather than testing backup-head takeover here. It also reports results on other tasks, which are not included unless they bear on an IOI claim version.
record.test_reason: The study's own GPT-2 small IOI experiments vary circuit-discovery method and settings: ACDC head order and ablation, EAP names, EP loss, and DiscoGP seeds. It reports that the recovered circuits differ sharply in structure, and that a component's indispensability depends on how the IOI prompt distribution is aggregated. This bears on V4 and V5. It never evaluates the original 26-head circuit, so V1, V2, V3 and V6 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a task such as IOI can be realised by multiple faithful, sparse, low-overlap circuits or sheaves across discovery methods. They also conclude that even a three-edge IOI sheaf has no indispensable edge once IOI is split into templates. Discovered mechanisms are one realisation among many, not the unique mechanism. They add a theoretical existence argument from superposition (the Distributive Dense Circuit Hypothesis).
record.recipe_differences: The study uses overlap-penalized DiscoGP sheaf discovery and evaluates competing sheaves, with additional ACDC, EAP, and EP comparisons. It evaluates masked graphs and edge overlap rather than reproducing the original study's head-role patching tests for the 26-head circuit.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with discovery method and its settings: ACDC attention-head traversal order and interchange versus zero ablation; EAP IOI names and retained-edge threshold k; EP task-specific CE versus full-vocabulary KL loss; and IOI aggregation versus ABBA/BABA decomposition.

fits_no_version.finding: IOI in GPT-2 small can be performed by many sparse edge-level sheaves (about 1000 edges, about 100% accuracy) with very low mutual overlap. A three-edge sheaf through L10H7 reaches 86.7%. Zero-ablating two of its edges in the full model drops accuracy to about 31%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: IOI-performing subgraphs in GPT-2 small are non-unique at edge level. Many structurally distinct sparse sheaves each sustain IOI in isolation.

fits_no_version.finding: DiscoGP finds low-overlap IOI sheaves in Pythia-160M, with about 80% average accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Edge-level non-uniqueness of IOI sheaves also appears in Pythia-160M.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The paper does not directly test the original 26-head circuit or its individual head roles. Numeric entries in the supplied Table 4 text are flattened ambiguously, so they are not assigned to particular ACDC measures. EAP overlap trends are shown in a figure without numeric values in the text. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the extracted results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 and Table 3 results for BLiMP, AGA, ANA, DNA variants, and Docstring, and the corresponding detailed appendices, are omitted because they concern other tasks rather than the IOI claim versions. Further per-sheaf rows in Tables 14-22 are omitted because the aggregate IOI results in Table 3 and representative individual IOI results cover the relevant findings.

untested.parts: All of it: the 26 heads, the 7 classes and their roles, and the faithfulness, completeness and minimality of that circuit are never evaluated. Sheaves built from other edges do not show the original circuit is unfaithful.
All of it: backup name-mover heads are only cited from prior work.
All of it: the Pythia-160M sheaves are not analysed for head classes or roles, and there are no checkpoints or task reuse.
No comparison against the original 26-head circuit. Head-level agreement is not tested: node-level IoU is 64.2% versus 4.1% at edge level.
Partial-explanation and completeness of the original circuit under its own metric (logit difference) are not tested.
Whether the original circuit carries ABBA, BABA, other templates or more names is not tested.

missing.what: Mixed-IOI sheaves with the three-edge core excluded: accuracy 52.3%, complement 48.2%
Pairwise IoU of two random-init DiscoGP IOI sheaves: 18.5%, both 100% accuracy
Node-level IoU of the paired IOI sheaves: 64.2%, versus 4.1% at edge level
ACDC Table 4 numbers: interchange 174/608 edges, 353.4 edges, 90.75%; zero 302/6951 edges, 2194.7 edges, 87.50%
Iterative intersection circuits reach over 90% accuracy at 11 edges while their complements stay near chance

record.verdict_notes: The paper argues against uniqueness framings, including Wang et al.'s, but never evaluates the 26-head circuit. Its edge-level sheaves share about 64% of nodes, so a head-level circuit could sit inside many of them. That is why V1 is left untested rather than challenged. Most sheaf results are zero-ablation; the about-31% (below-chance) accuracies from removing edges of L10H7 may reflect zero-ablation artefacts. The ACDC appendix says head order is the only randomness, although the main text mentions random seeds. OASR rows reflect a deliberate overlap penalty, so they are excluded from V4.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test the named 26 attention heads, their seven classes or stated roles, or the original circuit's faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria individually. Its evidence bears on whether the IOI account should be treated as a unique or essential mechanism.
The paper discusses backup name-mover heads from prior work but does not ablate the original main name-mover heads or measure self-repair.

The paper reports IOI sheaf results on Pythia-160M, but does not test whether the original head classes and roles recur across models, sizes, or checkpoints, or whether those components are reused for other tasks.
The study compares ACDC, EAP, and Edge Pruning (EP), but does not compare every circuit-finding method, ablation type, and metric named in the version.
The study examines ablation, discovery method, name changes, and task decomposition, but does not comprehensively vary all metrics or prompt distributions.

It examines ABBA and BABA template subsets under a constraint excluding the three-edge core. It does not test whether the original 26-head circuit carries the task across those formats, or examine more-name prompts.
